notes.meaning: Abram left Egypt and traveled up into the Negev, the dry southern part of Canaan. He brought his wife Sarai, all his belongings, and his nephew Lot along with him. Egypt was low land along the Nile River, while Canaan was higher country, so traveling there was an upward journey.

God had blessed Abram with enormous wealth during his time away, including large herds of animals, silver, and gold. In the ancient language of the Bible, being very rich literally meant being heavy or weighed down with goods. While his riches were a gift from God, they also brought more burdens and worries.

Abram moved in slow stages from pasture to pasture until he came to the hill country between Bethel and Ai. This was the exact area where he had pitched his tent when he first entered Canaan. Retracing his steps helped him return to the place where he had previously walked closely with God.

Abram arrived at the spot where he had previously built an altar, and there he openly worshiped the Lord. His original altar may have broken down or been removed while he was away in Egypt. He used this return to make a fresh start and thank God for keeping him safe through danger and famine.

Lot had traveled along with Abram and had also gained large flocks of sheep, herds of cattle, and tents. The mention of many tents shows that Lot now had a large group of servants and shepherds of his own. Both men had grown into wealthy leaders of powerful family clans.

The grazing land around Bethel was not large enough to feed the herds of both Abram and Lot at the same time. The ground may still have been dry from the recent famine, leaving pasture and water in short supply. Their great wealth made it impossible for their households to remain together peacefully in one place.

Arguments soon broke out between Abram's herdsmen and Lot's herdsmen over who would get the best wells and grazing grounds. This quarreling was dangerous because the local Canaanites and Perizzites were living nearby and watching them. A public family fight risked inviting an attack from their neighbors and brought dishonor to their faith.

Abram stepped forward to stop the arguing before it ruined his relationship with Lot. He urged Lot to avoid any fighting between them or their workers because they were close kin who worshiped the same God. Even though Abram was the older man with greater authority, he took the humble first step to make peace.

Abram generously gave Lot first choice of any part of the land for his flocks. If Lot chose the northern areas to the left, Abram would take the southern hills to the right, or the reverse. Abram trusted God to take care of him, so he did not feel the need to fight for the best ground.

Lot looked out over the Jordan Valley toward the town of Zoar and saw that the whole plain was green and richly watered. Before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, that valley was lush like the garden of Eden and fertile like the irrigated fields of Egypt. Lot chose his future purely based on what looked rich and pleasant to his eyes.

Lot picked the entire Jordan Valley for himself and set off toward the east. He did not show respect to his older uncle by offering him first choice, but greedily took what seemed best. With this decision, the two men separated their households and went their own ways.

Abram continued to live in the hill country of Canaan, dwelling in tents as a pilgrim. Lot moved down near the cities of the valley and gradually shifted his tents closer to the city of Sodom. While Abram chose a simple life of faith, Lot chose to settle near a corrupt city for worldly comfort.

The people living in Sodom were openly wicked and committed terrible sins against the Lord. Lot ignored the spiritual danger of the city because he was attracted by the wealth and beauty of the land. Moving toward ungodly company often leads to great sorrow.

After Lot had left, the Lord spoke to Abram to comfort him in his loss. God told him to look out from where he stood in all directions: north, south, east, and west. Though Abram had surrendered the valley to Lot, God reminded him that the entire land was still reserved for his own future.

God gave Abram an absolute promise that all the land he could see would belong to him and his family line forever. Abram held the legal right to the country by God's word, even while he lived there only as a guest in tents. God's gifts to his servants are lasting and secure.

differ.view: The promise is a literal and everlasting land grant to the physical descendants of Abraham through Jacob.
The physical land pointed to the eternal heavenly country, which belongs forever to all spiritual children of Abraham through faith in Christ.

notes.meaning: God told Abram that his descendants would become so numerous that they could no more be counted than the dust of the ground. This was an amazing word of hope for Abram, who was an old man with no children yet. It taught him to look beyond his present circumstances and rely on the power of God.

God instructed Abram to get up and walk through the length and width of the territory. In ancient customs, walking across a parcel of land was a legal way of claiming it and taking formal possession. Each journey Abram took was a quiet act of faith that God was giving that ground to his family.

Abram packed up his camp and moved south to live near the great oak trees of Mamre at Hebron. Mamre was a local Amorite chieftain who made a friendly agreement with Abram to live in peace. In this new home, Abram built an altar to worship the Lord with sacrifices and thank him for his promises.
